reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the wisdom sayings as claims about final, eternal outcome rather than literal life-span promises, so Job's observation and the maxims coexist.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogs this verse set, framing Job's admission against the wisdom books' insistence that the wicked's days are cut short.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/wicked_livelong.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: neither shall he prolong--not a contradiction to Ecc 8:12. The "prolonging" of his days there is only seeming, not real. Taking into account his eternal existence, his present days, however seemingly long, are really short. God's delay (Ecc 8:11) exists only in man's short-sighted view.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB explicitly denies a contradiction between the sinner's apparent long life and the claim his days are cut short, resolving it via a real/apparent and temporal/eternal distinction -- this is the exact mechanism harmonizers use for the whole cluster (Job's this-life report vs. the wisdom books' shortened-days maxims).

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Job 21:7
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry's extended note on Job 21:7 directly engages this tension -- conceding the wicked's real this-life prosperity against the friends' (and by extension, the wisdom tradition's) claims, and resolving it by appeal to a future 'world of retribution.' Haley's Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible does not treat Job 21 or this verse cluster (confirmed by a full-text search of the archive.org djvu.txt of examinationofall00hale -- no hits for 'Job xxi', 'wicked prosper', or related phrases), so the contract's named alternative (a harmonizing commentator already surfaced on the row, keyed to the passage) is used instead.
